 The best laptop power banks are a must-buy when you're working away from a power socket. After all, even the best laptops for photo editing won't run on battery forever. And with governments telling us all to stock up on food and prepare for power outages, a power bank is a great way of ensuring you can keep vital devices going for a few days if the mains electricity fails to flow.
 But, the best iPhone power banks won't be powerful enough to do the job. Instead, you'll need a power bank with at least 18,000mAh capacity, as well as the right ports to connect to your specific laptop.
 As an added bonus, with a power bank this powerful, you'll be able to charge your cameras, tablets, phones,and other devices too. To find you the best model for your needs, we've put our experts to work. They've been testing and reviewing power banks, as well as using them within their own workflows, in order to compile this list of the absolute best.
 Latest Videos From Digital Camera World 
 Watch full video here: 
 Here is a round-up of four big "power stations" that we have tested…

 Reasons to buy
 + Rugged and well-built
 + Fast charging with USB-C and DJI-specific adapters
 + Designed for drone users
 Reasons to avoid
 - No built-in light
 - No app or battery health monitor
 The DJI Power 1000 is a rugged, high-capacity power station designed with drone users in mind. With 1,024Wh of capacity and 2,200W continuous output (4,400W peak), it provides ample power for charging multiple drone batteries, cameras, and other essential gear on location. The two USB-C ports (140W each) allow for fast charging, while the SDC and SDC Lite ports support DJI’s proprietary adapters for even more efficient drone charging.
 Weighing 13kg, the Power 1000 is not the lightest option, but its sturdy build and rounded handles make it easy to carry. The clear display offers essential battery information, though it lacks smart features like an app or battery health monitoring. Additionally, there’s no built-in light or wireless charging, which could be a drawback for some users.
 Despite these limitations, the DJI Power 1000 excels at providing reliable, high-wattage power for drone operators and creatives working off-grid. Whether you're filming in remote locations or need a dependable backup power source, this station delivers efficient, high-speed charging for DJI drones and other kit.

 The best laptop power bank overall
 Our expert review:

 Reasons to buy
 + Charge up to 5 devices
 + Huge capacity
 + Compact unit
 Reasons to avoid
 - Heavy to carry around
 - Lacks a charging plug
 Want the best power bank that will fit in your pocket? We reckon that's the UGREEN 300W 48,000mAh; a robust and high-capacity portable charger designed for users seeking extensive device charging capabilities.
 This power bank stands out for two main reasons. One is its impressive 48,000mAh capacity, which makes it capable of charging an iPhone 15 Pro nearly 11 times. The second is its ability to charge up to five devices at the same time, with a maximum output of 300W. That makes it particularly well-suited for camping trips, weekend hikes, or emergency power situations.
 Despite its somewhat hefty weight of 1.86 kg, the power bank features a sleek design with high-quality materials, including a low-light display that provides real-time information about battery level and power input/output. Equipped with two USB-A ports and three USB-C ports, the power bank offers versatile charging options.
 It's likely to last you a while too; Ugreen claims the device will retain 80% of its capacity after 3,000 charge cycles. However, our reviewer also noted a few drawbacks, such as its heavy weight, the lack of an included charging plug, and variable charging speeds depending on the cables used.

 Reasons to buy
 + Fast charging speeds (if your device supports them)
 + Numerical charge indicator
 + Big capacity
 Reasons to avoid
 - Remembering all the charging output combinations can be confusing
 If your primary concern is charging your PD devices as fast as possible then this power bank from UGREEN is for you. Capable of 145W power split across its USB ports, with one 100W capable USB-C, it's ready for all your devices that can be fast charged, as well as laptops that need lots of juice, and it's also future-proofed for those devices that haven't come along yet. With enough capacity to charge your phone several times over, or run your camera and accessories off while on long shoots away from a constant power supply.
 However it isn't the only 25,000mAh capacity power bank on the market, so if you don't need its fast charging powers then you can get cheaper and lighter options elsewhere (or from UGREEN themselves), and the complex and varying power outputs might just be enough to put a lot of people off.
 Read more: UGREEN 145W Power Bank review 
 (Image credit: Gareth Bevan / Digital Camera World) 4. Anker Prime 20,000mAh Power Bank (200W) 
 The best laptop power bank display
 Our expert review:

 Maximum wattage: 100W (200W total)

 Reasons to buy
 + Two simultaneous 100W fast charging outputs
 + Useful informative screen
 + Decent battery capacity
 + Looks great
 Reasons to avoid
 - Not the biggest battery
 - Boxy design makes it harder to slip into pockets
 You don't really need to have an informative screen on your power bank, but the Anker Prime power bank has the easiest power percentage and countdown timer for charging/discharging the battery I have used yet. And knowing exactly how fast my laptop is charging is both just plain interesting to know, but I can also plan ahead to give make sure I have enough juice left throughout the day.
 The Anker Prime power isn’t just about a screen though, it also has a solid 20,000mAh of battery which I managed to get a few days' worth of keeping my phone and laptop going with short bursts of recharging, or one big recharge of my MacBook Pro 13. The big 200W maximum output, with a 100W single port output, also allowed me to use my laptop at full power. The power bank is a little boxy for slipping into pockets, but it looks great.
 Read more: Anker Prime 20,000mAh Power Bank (200W) review 
 FAQs 
 Will one of the best portable chargers work for a laptop?
 Sadly not, you will need a power bank with a much higher capacity than most power banks used to charge camera phones or other small appliances. It's recommended that you invest in a power bank with a 20,000 mAh or larger especially if you want to charge it multiple times. 
 How do I connect my laptop to the powerbank?
 How you connect your laptop to your power bank will depend on the time of charging cable your laptop needs. While most modern laptops such as the Apple Macbook Pro 14 M2 will have a USB C input, some older models might still use round AC adapters or a standard USB A input. You will be able to get the correct cable from Amazon.

 Well, it's official: there are two new kids on the block. The new MacBook Pro M6 and the MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen are finally here. If you've been waiting to upgrade, or are looking to pick up your first-ever MacBook, now's the time to do it. Pre-orders are live , and we've even found a trick to help you save up to $1,400 on the OLED model .
 As someone who owns a MacBook and uses one for work, and coincidentally tests the latest and greatest peripherals, I know that your setup isn't complete until you buy the right accessories. I couldn't get on with my work without my trusty mouse, keyboard, monitor, and other gadgets.
 Whether you're after a new mechanical keyboard or even a touch-sensitive one whose keycaps double as a trackpad, a pair of earbuds, or need a USB-C dock for more connectivity, I've got you covered. I've rounded up what I believe are the best accessories (and gadgets) to make the most of your new MacBook Pro M6 or OLED.
 New MacBook Pro pre-orders 
 OLED touchscreen
 MacBook Pro OLED 14-inch: $2,899 at Apple The MacBook Pro OLED is one of the biggest MacBook releases in recent years. It can be configured with an M5 Pro (from $2,899) or M5 Max (from $4,499) CPU and packs a 14.2-inch PROLED XDR touchscreen display with 3024 x 1986 resolution, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB SSD. You also get three Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports, HDMI port, and an SDXC slot. The laptop will be available on November 6. 
 View Deal 
 M6 chip
 MacBook Pro M6 14-inch: $1,999 at Amazon Power users looking for a boost in performance should opt for the new 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro. This powerful laptop sports Apple's M6 chip for blazing-fast performance at home or on the go.
 View Deal 
 Monitor 
 27-inch
 Apple Studio Display: was $1,569 now $1,519 at BHPhoto There's no better monitor for your new MacBook Pro than the first-party Apple Studio Display, thanks to its excellent 12MP ultra-wide camera, fantastic six-speaker setup and gorgeous 27-inch 5K screen. It's bright and delivers accurate (and stunning) colors, too.
 Read our full Apple Studio Display review . 
 View Deal 
 27-inch
 BenQ MA270S: $999 at benq.com If you don't mind a third-party display, I can't recommend the BenQ MA270S enough. It's cheaper than the Apple Studio Display and boasts wide color coverage and excellent accuracy, making it a great choice for creatives, and it comes with an Apple-like app for customization. There’s no shortage of ports, and the Nano Gloss 5K panel is a sight to behold.
 Read my full BenQ MA270S review . 
 View Deal 
 40-inch
 Alogic Edge 5K: $1,699 at Adorama If you want more screen real estate, the Alogic Edge 40-inch 5K is an excellent choice. Boasting great color coverage and accuracy, and hosting a plethora of ports for Mac users, this monitor offers everything you could ask for. Available in Silver and Space Gray, it’ll fit right into your existing Mac-first setup, too.
 Read my full Alogic Edge 5K review . 
 View Deal 
 Keyboard 
 Touch-sensitive
 Clevetura S: $199 at Amazon The Clevetura S is an outstanding travel-friendly keyboard with touch-sensitive keycaps that turn it into a highly effective and responsive trackpad with MacBook gestures, negating the need for a separate mouse. Its scissor switches are great to type on, too.
 Read my full Clevetura S review . 
 View Deal 
 100% layout
 Keychron K10 Max: $119 at Amazon The K10 Max is a fantastic iteration of the tried-and-true Keychron formula, offering additional sound dampening, a refined mounting system, and high-performance Super Switches. A deep, thick sound and responsive keystrokes make this a great gaming option, too. It comes with macOS keycaps, making it a solid choice for Apple users.
 Read our full Keychron K10 Max review . 
 View Deal 
 75% layout
 Epomaker Glyph: was $139 now $132 at Amazon Want a keyboard that looks a bit different? The typewriter-like Epomaker Glyph (featuring macOS keycaps) is a wonderful, whimsical addition to any setup. It puts the joy back into typing. The keyboard sports a charming typewriter-like design with dual screens and customizable RGB lighting, and build quality is solid.
 Read my full Epomaker Glyph review . 
 View Deal 
 Mouse 
 Touch-sensitive
 Apple Magic Mouse (USB-C): $79 at BHPhoto There's no better mouse for the MacBook other than the Apple Magic Mouse (as long as you don't mind the very flat design). It features a Multi-Touch surface that allows you to perform gestures, and the mouse can last up to a month between charges. This model features a USB-C port. On the bottom.
 View Deal 
 Ergonomic
 BenQ INFTYLAB M Mouse PS01: $119 at BHPhoto If you want an ergonomic mouse with buttons that toggle macOS shortcuts, try the BenQ INFTYLAB M Mouse PS01. It features dual scrolling wheels, smooth tracking, and you can assign macOS gestures to its buttons. User-friendly companion software makes customization easy, too.
 Read my full BenQ INFTYLAB M Mouse PS01 review . 
 View Deal 
 Gaming
 Corsair M75 (Mac): $129 at Apple Given how powerful both the MacBook Pro M6 and OLED sound, I won't be surprised if they're great for gaming. The Corsair M75 (Mac) is a superb gaming mouse designed for macOS. This minimalist-looking mouse features 26,000 DPI sensitivity that you can change on the fly, making it suitable for all kinds of gaming titles. It’s very comfortable to use for long hours.
 Read my full Corsair M75 (Mac) review . 
 View Deal 
 Dock 
 Desk-made
 UGREEN 8-in-1 Thunderbolt 4 Docking Station: was $249 now $169 at Amazon The UGREEN 8-in-1 Thunderbolt 4 Docking Station is a must-have for those who have a desk setup. It's equipped with three Thunderbolt 4 ports (40Gbps, 15W), three USB-A ports (10Gbps), a gigabit ethernet port, and a 140W DC power port. It's great for creatives and professionals who need high transfer speeds.
 View Deal 
 Portable
 Anker 8-in-1 USB-C Hub: $53 at Amazon I couldn't live without my portable USB-C hub. The Anker 8-in-1 USB-C Hub is ideal for those on the move. It features multiple USB-C and USB-A ports, as well as HDMI 4K/60Hz ports for streaming and mirroring content. There are also two SD and microSD card slots — perfect for photographers and videographers.
 View Deal 
 Stand 
 Fixed, non-adjustable
 Twelve South Curve Stand: $59 at Apple The Twelve South Curve Stand sports a modern and minimal design that complements and enhances your MacBook and workspace. It raises your screen off the desk for improved ergonomics and airflow.
 View Deal 
 Adjustable
 Twelve South Curve Flex Stand: $79 at Apple The Twelve South Curve Flex Stand elevates your MacBook up to 22 inches and adjusts your keyboard angle from zero to 45°, resulting in a more ergonomic and comfortable viewing and typing experience. It folds flat so you can take it with you when you travel.
 View Deal 
 Earbuds 
 Open-ear
 Apple AirPods 5: $129 at Best Buy If you have an existing Apple ecosystem (iPhone, iPad, MacBook, etc.), the Apple AirPods 5 are an excellent choice. Starting from just $124, these affordable earbuds are the ideal model those on a budget. While the battery life is abysmal, the sound quality, comfort, fit, smart features, and ANC make up for it for casual users.
 Read our full Apple AirPods 5 review . 
 View Deal 
 Sealed in-ear
 Apple AirPods 3 Pro: was $249 now $199 at Amazon If you need AirPods that don't skimp on features, the AirPods Pro 3 are the ones for you. They pack useful features like heart rate monitor and Live Translation. The fit is fantastic and comfortable, and there's plenty of battery to keep them going for long listening sessions.
 Read our full Apple AirPods Pro 3 review . 
 View Deal 
 Over-ear
 Apple AirPods Max 2: was $549 now $449 at Amazon Stuffed full of AirPods Pro-esque features like Head Gestures, Live Translation, Camera Remote, and improved Siri integration, the AirPods Max 2 pack lots of smart tech features alongside sound that's rich, complex, and most importantly, fun.
 Read our full Apple AirPods Max 2 review . 
 View Deal 
 Sleeve 
 14-inch or 16-inch
 TomToc 360 Protective Sleeve: $42 at Amazon The TomToc 360 Protective Sleeve is a must-have for those who want to protect their new MacBook Pro M6 or OLED when they're traveling. With four corner protectors, resilient edges, high-density padding, and water-resistant fabric, it protects your laptop from inevitable bumps, scratches and water spills. It also has two separate compartments with several small pockets and a strap for an AirTag or key.
 View Deal 
 14-inch or 16-inch
 Rains Laptop Portfolio: $80 at Apple If you want a more low-key sleeve, the Rains Laptop Portfolio waterproof sleeve is sleek and good-looking. It features a flap closure fastened with concealed magnetic straps, and it's made of durable and smooth PU fabric.
 View Deal

That's why my team of experts and I have done extensive hands-on testing for picture quality, color accuracy, connectivity and more for each monitor to help you find the right fit for your desk.
 Right now, we highly recommend the Philips 27E3U7903 as the best monitor for MacBook Pro for most, as this 5K beauty ticks all the right boxes and is far less expensive than Apple's Studio Display (even though that is still a great choice).  The Philips 27E3U7903 takes the crown as our top pick for MacBook Pro users who want a monitor that nails modern connectivity and delivers a true high-res experience without the Apple tax. In our testing, we found it needs to be excellent across the board to justify its premium price, and the combination of practical features and 5K clarity gets it most of the way there.
 Connectivity is where the 27E3U7903 shines. With HDMI 2.1, a Thunderbolt 4 port delivering 96W of Power Delivery (enough to fully charge a MacBook Pro), plus additional Thunderbolt, USB-C, and USB-A ports, it handles single-cable docking, peripheral charging, and daisy chaining with ease. We found the built-in KVM switch and multi-port options made switching between devices and tidying up desk clutter genuinely seamless.
 On the visual front, you’re getting a 5K (5120 x 2880) panel using IPS Black tech, meaning crisp, retina-style sharpness for macOS, vibrant colors, and a punchy backlight. In hands-on use, the panel’s vibrancy and power stood out, making it suitable for everything from spreadsheets to creative work, even if it won’t quite match Apple on calibration out of the box.
 Yes, the Apple Studio Display still wins for build quality and Mac integration, but the Philips matches its resolution and undercuts it on price. So you aren’t paying for the logo.
 If you’re looking for a premium-feeling, high-resolution monitor that offers practical one-cable MacBook Pro docking, the 27E3U7903 is a strong choice. You’ll give up some of Apple’s design polish and factory calibration, but for most users after ports, clarity, and versatility, it’s the best all-rounder we’ve tested.

 Best monitor for MacBook Pro: FAQs 
 (Image credit: Acer // Future) What is the best resolution for monitors with a MacBook Pro?
 The MacBook Pro is Apple's machine for creators, and that means having excellent visuals for photo and video editing, 3D creative work, and more. To make the most out of what you work on, 4K (3840 x 2160) resolution is the way to go. That said, if you're using your MacBook Pro for anything else, like spreadsheets, writing documents or even coding, you'll be just fine with even a 1080p display. If you're after the highest pixel density, though, 5K and upwards is what you're after. 
 What Power Delivery should the monitor have to charge my MacBook Pro?
 You'll see many monitors with Thunderbolt/USB-C Power Delivery (PD). This means you can plug your MacBook Pro into the monitor and it will charge the laptop while in use. 
 However, the right choice depends on your MacBook Pro's model and CPU. Check out the table below to see which one is right for your laptop.

 Are there any specific connectivity options that I should look for in a monitor for my MacBook Pro?
 The best monitors for a MacBook Pro will feature USB-C and/or Thunderbolt connectivity. These allow slick, single-cable connectivity that covers charging the MacBook, driving the display, and connecting peripherals. 
 Outside of that, you can find a monitor with a built-in USB-C hub that opens up several ports through the single USB-C used to send video to your monitor. Depending on the monitor, sometimes this can also be used to charge your MacBook Pro.
 Are there any monitors that are specifically designed for use with the MacBook Pro?
 Some monitors, such as the Apple Studio Display and Apple Pro Display XDR, are explicitly designed for use with Apple devices and mirror the wide color P3 gamut and Liquid Retina Display. 
 However, many high-quality monitors from other brands are also compatible with the MacBook Pro. Some monitors will work better with the MacBook Pro than others, but generally, any even semi-recent monitor will be compatible in one way or another with a MacBook Pro.
 How to choose the best monitor for MacBook Pro 
 When choosing which monitor is best for your MacBook Pro, there are a few specs and details you'll want to check.
 Not everyone will need the same specifications. For example, if you're mostly working with office apps, you may not need the broader color space coverage that's required for image or video editing. However you use your monitor, here's what we recommend looking out for.
 Resolution : macOS loves high-resolution displays. The more pixels, the better for rendering nice, clean fonts and providing plenty of image detail. Apple's own desktop displays, the Apple Pro Display XDR and Studio Display, have what's known as Retina pixel density. In practice, that means over 200 pixels per inch (PPI), which matches the screens in the MacBook Pro. Very few non-Apple displays can match that pixel density, but a 27-inch 4K display with 163 pixels per inch is a good baseline.
 Connectivity : USB-C or Thunderbolt with Power Delivery is the bare minimum when it comes to connectivity. We'd recommend at least 65W of power delivery and ideally 90W-plus for keeping your MacBook Pro fully powered. A USB hub with plenty of USB-A and USB-C ports is very desirable, too. Additional inputs like HDMI can be handy, and an Ethernet port can be useful for some office environments. The ability to daisy chain a second monitor is also an interesting option, as is a KVM switch if you're sharing the display with a second computer.
 HDR versus SDR support: HDR is a tricky technology. Many workflows don't require it. But it is becoming more widespread. A display with HDR capability tends to also offer increased colour coverage and generally improve image quality. However, the technologies that enable HDR rendering vary hugely, and some displays are much more effective than others. For that reason, unless you know your workflows require full HDR support, we recommend focusing on getting a display with good SDR performance. If it happens to also offer some HDR capability, great. But for most users, HDR probably isn't a top priority.
 Build quality and extras: It's easy to obsess over specifications like resolution and HDR performance. But the overall quality of a display and feature set can make a big difference, too. If you're paying big bucks, it's nice to have a display that feels worth the money and looks good with your laptop. Likewise, superficially lesser features like good speakers, a great webcam and a microphone array can make a big difference to the overall usability of a monitor. Having features like that built in can also help to reduce desk clutter and simplify docking and connectivity. For more extras, we've reviewed the best MacBook Pro accessories .
 How we test the best monitors for MacBook Pro 
 (Image credit: Future) Our expert team of reviewers has tested a massive range of displays, including the best monitors for photo editing and the best monitors for video editing . So, we're experienced at knowing what to look out for to help you find the best dual monitor set-up to go with your laptop.
 A decent monitor for your MacBook Pro isn't going to be cheap. So, you want to know you're making the right choice. That's why we test each display extensively. That starts with performance assessments of various aspects of image quality.
 That includes brightness, refresh rate, and pixel response. We also consider colour accuracy, viewing angles, contrast, HDR performance, latency, and last but by no means least, resolution and pixel density. Display tech is increasingly varied and complex, what with new technologies like HDR, mini-LED backlights, and OLED panels revolutionising the industry. So, we keep on top of all of that for you, helping you to understand the difference between a few edge-lit dimming zones and a real full-array deal
 Crucially, we also assess how well a display works with macOS. Once connected to a MacBook Pro, does it offer a full range of optimised scaling options, for instance? Next up is connectivity. We consider the range of ports on offer and whether single-cable docking with power delivery is included, along with USB hubs and other features like Ethernet, a KVM switch, and display daisy chaining.
 We also consider any extra features like webcams and speakers. In theory, they can add significant value. But if they're not done well, you're probably just paying for things you'll hardly ever use. You might even end up paying twice if you find you need to buy a dedicated webcam or speakers.
 Next up, there's build quality, design, and ergonomics. A monitor that looks great on the desk with your MacBook Pro is important. But good build quality matters, too. When you are investing a lot of money, you want a display to not just look good, but feel good and last the test of time.
 Then there's ergonomics. At a minimum, a robust and stable stand with a good range of adjustability, including height and tilt, is important. The ability to rotate into portrait mode can be handy, too.
 Of course, how all of those factors fit into the overall value proposition is the final measure. The MacBook Pro is a demanding machine. So, you're not going to get the best out of it with a budget display. But you can also spend a lot of money and not necessarily get a better display solution. We'll help you work out what's worth the money and what costs plenty but doesn't improve your macOS experience.

The right pick depends on whether you need all-day portability for work or study, serious gaming and creative performance, a repairable machine you can upgrade, or an affordable device for everyday browsing and streaming.
 At Tom's Guide, we’ve tested the leading options across those needs to help you find the best fit. The MacBook Air M5 remains our top all-round choice, with its powerful everyday performance, lightweight design and excellent battery life for the price. But there are other options if you want a Windows machine, a dedicated gaming rig, exceptional battery life, a laptop built for AI or for upgradeability.
 The MacBook PROLED and M6 MacBook Pro are now official, and these are already looking to be serious contenders for this guide.  Best Laptops: Frequently Asked Questions 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Should I buy a MacBook, Windows laptop or a Chromebook?
 Buy a MacBook if you are comfortable using Macs or are already embedded in the Apple ecosystem. While macOS is not as robust as Windows when it comes to gaming, many people find it easy to use and it's tightly integrated with Apple's other products, so your iPhone, iPad and AirPods will seamlessly work with your Mac.
 Buy a Windows 11 laptop if you need access to the widest selection of apps, are not tied down to any particular ecosystem, want the best gaming experience and are looking for the broadest selection of laptop designs. Only Windows laptops come with features like touchscreens, high-speed displays or the option to transform into a tablet. However, they typically have worse battery life than MacBooks. 
 Buy a Chromebook or Googlebook if your work and entertainment needs revolve entirely around a browser, Android or Gemini AI. If everything you do is within a Chrome browser or Google apps, then a Chromebook or higher-tier Googlebook is the most direct way to get there. Just be aware you'll be limited without internet — ChromeOS and Googlebook OS are robust operating systems, but without internet access, they can't do much.
 How much should I spend on a good laptop?
 Spend enough to match your workload, rather than paying for power or features you will not use. The best budget laptops can handle browsing, documents and streaming; mainstream laptops offer a better balance of portability and multitasking; and premium machines make sense for demanding creative work, gaming or maximum battery life.
 Our budget picks, the MacBook Neo and Dell XPS 13 , suit everyday tasks, while models such as the MacBook Air M5 and Dell XPS 14 are stronger all-round choices. Gaming and professional creative laptops cost more because they need faster components, more memory and better cooling. Prices and discounts change regularly, so compare the current configurations and avoid treating a temporary deal as a permanent price point.
 How much RAM do I need?
 For a modern laptop, 16GB of RAM is a sensible target for smooth everyday use and multitasking. It gives web browsers, office apps and background processes more room to run together, and is a better long-term choice than 8GB where the budget allows. Of course, with the RAM crisis , this is getting trickier, but with the right laptop, 8GB of RAM can take you far (as the MacBook Neo and Dell XPS 13 have shown us). 
 Choose more memory if you edit video, work with 3D projects, run demanding creative software, stream while gaming or regularly keep many intensive apps open. We recommend 32GB as a minimum for especially heavy 3D animation and streaming workloads. RAM is often not upgradeable on a laptop after purchase, so select the configuration you expect to need over the laptop’s useful life.
 What is an SSD, and how much storage do I need?
 An SSD is fast, flash-based storage that holds your operating system, apps and files; 256GB is a workable starting point, while 512GB gives most people more comfortable room. Unlike older mechanical hard drives, SSDs have no moving parts and are generally quicker and more robust for everyday laptop use.
 Choose 512GB or more if you keep large photo libraries or offline files on the laptop. Cloud storage and external SSDs can reduce the need for built-in capacity, but they are less convenient when travelling. For gaming and video projects, we suggest getting 1TB or more, as these large files can take up a lot of space fast. 
 What battery life should I look for in a laptop?
 Look for a laptop with enough battery life we've tested to cover your normal day away from a socket, rather than relying only on a manufacturer’s claim. Around a full work or study day is a useful goal for many buyers, but the right target depends on your workload, screen settings and how often you travel. As a good rule of thumb, if a laptop lasts over 10 hours, it's doing a good job. 
 In our testing, the MacBook Air M5 lasted more than 15 hours, the Dell XPS 13 more than 14 hours, and the MacBook Pro 16-inch M5 Pro more than 21 hours in its battery test. Gaming is much more demanding: the ROG Zephyrus G14 records far shorter gaming endurance, so plan to carry a charger for intensive use.
 Which accessories should I buy?
 Start with accessories that improve comfort and connectivity: a laptop stand, a mouse and, if required, a USB hub or dock. A stand can raise the screen to a more comfortable height, while a mouse is often more comfortable for long work sessions than relying on a trackpad. Check out our guide to the best mouse for more options. 
 Check your laptop’s ports and charging requirements before buying a hub or dock, especially with slim ultraportables that may offer only USB-C connections. A hub can add useful connections for displays, storage, keyboards and wired networking, but it must support the standards and power delivery your laptop needs. Buy additional accessories only for a genuine use case, such as one of the best monitors as an extra screen to have, a travel case or extra storage.

 Work and productivity: If your first priority is having an easy-to-carry PC you can use to answer email, prep documents and get work done on the go, you want a modern ultraportable that's light, comfy to use and offers great battery life. I generally recommend the MacBook Air M5 (macOS) or the Dell XPS 14 (Windows 11) for this, since they're both light, capable and long-lasting. You'll also find the Lenovo Googlebook 15 makes for an excellent lightweight addition. If you're technical and like the idea of upgrading and repairing your own laptop, I wholeheartedly recommend you check out the Framework Laptop instead, since you can modify and upgrade it for as long as you own it, in a way that no other laptop can match.
 Gaming: If you plan to spend a lot of time gaming, you want a laptop with a speedy CPU, a discrete laptop graphics card and plenty of RAM. If you plan to play at higher than 60 frames per second, a screen with a high refresh rate is also critical. Personally, I recommend the Asus ROG Zephyrus G14 since it satisfies all these requirements while remaining pretty portable, but if you adore macOS, the MacBook Pro M5 is also pretty good for gaming if you restrict yourself to games optimized for Apple Silicon. But now, you can also play the latest titles with a laptop like the Dell XPS 14 , Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra and Asus ProArt P16 with RTX Spark.
 Creative work: If you plan to do a lot of 3D work, audio/video editing or demanding content creation, you will want a laptop with a powerful CPU, a discrete GPU (or powerful integrated graphics) and plenty of RAM to handle demanding workloads. In that sense, you want something like a gaming laptop (but ideally with better battery life and lighter weight), and you also want a sharp, color-accurate screen. This is why I generally recommend the MacBook Pro M5 , Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra and Asus ProArt P16 for such uses.
 Casual use: If you just need a laptop for basic writing, browsing the web and binge-watching YouTube or your favorite shows, you can save yourself a lot of money with a budget-friendly laptop. I recommend the MacBook Neo if you prefer macOS, the Dell XPS 13 for Windows or the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 if you're okay with a Chromebook and have reliable access to Wi-Fi (because Chromebooks can't do much without an internet connection).
 ▲ Back to the top 
 How we test laptops 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) In our never-ending quest to find the best laptops, I put every computer we test through a barrage of synthetic and real-world tests to benchmark how well it performs compared to the manufacturer's claims, and compare how good it is relative to the competition.
 These tests include, but are not limited to: measuring the average brightness and color quality of each laptop's display using our in-house colorimeter, using a heat gun to measure the heat generated by the laptop after 15 minutes of strenuous work, and using a mix of real-world and synthetic benchmarks to test how well a laptop performs at various day-to-day tasks.
 I put all laptops through the Geekbench CPU performance benchmark tests as well as various 3DMark tests to measure graphics capabilities. I also run a file transfer test to measure how fast a machine's hard drive is, a video transcoding test to gauge how well a laptop can cut video and a custom battery test that has the machine browse the internet over Wi-Fi until it runs out of juice.
 There are also gaming benchmarks that I use — testing a basic game like Sid Meier's Civilization VI: Gathering Storm to gauge how good it is at running games compared to other laptops. I use this old game because it runs on a wide variety of laptops across different prices, sizes and operating systems, so it's great for comparing performance.
 Of course, when testing dedicated gaming laptops, I run benchmarks for many more demanding and popular games, including Assassin's Creed Shadows, Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong . For more information on our testing process, check out our guide to how we test .

 Apple has just announced two new flagship laptops: the MacBook Pro OLED and the MacBook Pro M6 . The former is the company’s first touchscreen OLED MacBook, while the latter updates last year’s MacBook Pro M5 . Both should be fantastic laptops for pro users, but which one should you buy?
 We haven't tested either of these new MacBooks yet, but based on what we know, they shouldn’t have trouble landing on our best MacBooks page.
 To that end, here’s everything you need to know about the MacBook Pro OLED and MacBook Pro M6 to help you decide which one is right for you. Also, be sure to read our hands-on with the MacBook Pro OLED from the Apple "Pro and Tell" event !

 MacBook Pro OLED vs MacBook Pro M6: Price 
 (Image credit: Apple edited with Gemini) There’s no denying that both new MacBook models cost a pretty penny. That said, one is definitely more affordable than the other (relatively speaking).
 The 14-inch MacBook Pro OLED with the M5 Pro chip, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch model with the same specs starts at $3,399. If you want a laptop with the M5 Max chip, the 14-inch model starts at $4,499, while the 16-inch model is $4,799.
 You may like
 MacBook Pro M6 vs MacBook Pro M5: Biggest upgrades you need to know 
 Apple reveals OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro with Dynamic Island and M5 Pro power in 3-pound design 
 Should you buy the touchscreen MacBook Pro? 10 things you need to know 
 Then we have the 14-inch MacBook Pro, which starts at $1,999 and packs an M6 chip with a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, 16GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage. You can add up to 32GB of RAM and 4TB of storage, though that’ll substantially bring up the price.
 MacBook Pro OLED vs MacBook Pro M6: Display 
 (Image credit: Future) The biggest difference between these two MacBooks is their respective displays. The MacBook Pro OLED is the first MacBook with a touchscreen OLED panel, while the MacBook Pro M6 keeps the mini-LED screen of current MacBooks. Depending on what you want or need, this could be the main determining factor in which MacBook you’d buy.
 Want more Apple news?
 Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.
 According to Apple, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display “offers a visual experience unlike any other." That’s no doubt because of the tandem OLED panel, which promises true per-pixel blacks and zero blooming around UI elements.
 Apple claims this display can deliver peak SDR and HDR brightness of 2000 nits, which is absolutely eye-scorching. Apple says the tandem OLED technology keeps brightness and grayscale uniform across the entire display. The company also says it precisely calibrates each display for consistency.
 On top of that—and I mean that literally—the notch cutout at the top of the panel has been replaced by the Dynamic Island you’ve seen on the best iPhones . This brings Live Activities to the MacBook for the first time.
 What to read next
 We predicted the OLED MacBook Pro's $500 price hike — here's what the leaks say and why MacBook Air buyers may miss out 
 Apple MacBook Pro M6 just unveiled with 30% faster graphics, 25% faster AI and up to 24 hours of battery life 
 Which MacBook should you buy in 2026? I ranked the 5 best Apple laptops for every need 
 Lastly, the MacBook Pro OLED has a touchscreen. Apple says it crafted touch input specifically for the Mac, with a touch sensor built directly into the display panel, not layered on top. Our own Mark Spoonauer went hands-on with the MacBook Pro OLED and said that the touchscreen support feels “pretty smooth” as he navigated between apps or used his finger to draw. However, it doesn’t support the Apple Pencil.

 Apple didn’t update the MacBook Pro M6's Liquid Retina XDR display, so we already have a good idea of what it can do based on our testing and experience with previous models. Specifically, it has a 14.2-inch Mini-LED display running at 120Hz ProMotion, with a notch cutout at the top and no Dynamic Island-like functionality.
 Since the display is the same, our benchmarks for the MacBook Pro M5 should be virtually identical on the new model. That means you’ll get excellent color representation (sRGB and DCI-P3) and color accuracy (Delta E). Even without an OLED, the M6 MacBook Pro’s mini-LED panel should be stunning.
 MacBook Pro OLED vs MacBook Pro M6: Design 
 (Image credit: Future) MacBook Pros have featured the same design since late 2021, but the new MacBook Pro OLED finally ends that streak. While the new design might not be radically different, the changes introduced should make for a laptop that’s easier to travel with.
 Because OLED panels don’t require the same backlight array, the MacBook Pro OLED is thinner and lighter than current MacBook Pros. The 14-inch model weighs half a pound less at 3 pounds, while the 16-inch model is just a tad over four pounds. With slimmer borders, the 16-inch display grows to 16.3 inches, while the 14-inch display stays at a more portable 14.2 inches.
 (Image credit: Future) Port-wise, the MacBook Pro packs three Thunderbolt 5 ports, an HDMI port, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe, and a headphone jack. It supports up to three external displays with M5 Pro and up to four with M5 Max. It also supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. The M6 MacBook Pro has the same port selection, though the USB-C ports are Thunderbolt 4 instead of Thunderbolt 5.
 Last but certainly not least, the MacBook Pro OLED resurrects the classic glowing Apple logo on the lid. We haven’t seen this design feature for over eight years, so it’s a nice callback for long-time Apple fans.
 MacBook Pro OLED vs MacBook Pro M6: Performance 
 (Image credit: Future) One of the more intriguing things about the MacBook Pro OLED is that it utilizes the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips found in the existing MacBook Pro models. But while the 14-inch MacBook Pro packs the new M6 chip that first debuted in the new Mac mini M6 , the “older” M5 Pro/Max processors are actually more powerful.
 We haven't tested the new MacBook Pros yet, but based on our testing of MacBook Pros with M5 Pro and M5 Max, along with benchmarks of the M6 Mac mini, we have a sense of what to expect in terms of performance. Just keep in mind that differences will exist because the chips power different hardware.

 Pro and Max versions of M-series chips are always the most powerful in the line, even outperforming the entry-level version of newer chips. Because of that, we expect that the MacBook Pro OLED will be noticeably more powerful than the MacBook Pro M6.
 MacBook Pro OLED vs MacBook Pro M6: Outlook 
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) With both new MacBooks launching on November 6, we won’t have to wait long to see what they can truly do. That said, based on what we know so far, it’s not too hard to decide which notebook to buy.
 If you’ve been waiting for a MacBook Pro with an OLED screen and touchscreen support, consider the MacBook Pro OLED. Just keep its sticker price in mind, as it’s currently the most expensive MacBook available.
 Conversely, if touchscreen support and OLED aren’t as important, then you won’t go wrong with the M6 MacBook Pro. This is especially true if you want to save nearly $1,000 off the starting price. And while an OLED touchscreen is certainly enticing, the MacBook Pro M6's Mini-LED panel won’t disappoint.

 It’s important to note that there are risks with buying a cheap charger and we don’t recommend you choose on price alone. That bargain MacBook charger might just fry your laptop or get dangerously hot. However, there are some great premium chargers from trusted brands that sell for less than Apple pricey chargers. All the chargers listed here have been tested and are trusted by Macworld.
 What to look for in a MacBook charger
 PD charging 
 What you need is a Power Delivery (PD) charger that can connect to your MacBook via USB-C. The most common congregate around the standard laptop power requirements: 30W, 45W, 65W, 100W and 140W. All the USB-C chargers tested here are PD chargers and can also fast-charge an iPhone or even your Watch and AirPods.
 PD version 3.0 supports up to 100W. PD 3.1 can charge at 140W, which is what you need to fast-charge a 16-inch MacBook Pro. Note that most Thunderbolt 4 ports are rated at PD 3.0—only newer Thunderbolt 5 and the MacBook’s MagSafe port are PD 3.1 so you must use the Apple USB-C to MagSafe 3 Cable to fast-charge the models of the 140W 16-inch MacBook Pro older than the M4 versions. You can still power those non-M4 laptops via USB-C or Thunderbolt cable but 100W is the maximum power via that method.
 Wattage 
 A laptop is designed to draw up to a certain amount of watts when running at full power; that is when you are stretching it by using lots of apps or pushing the graphics and video rendering functions—not when you’re just browsing the web. Apple considers this level of max power when it decides on the wattage of the charger it includes with the MacBook. When the laptop is idle or doing mundane jobs, it will draw only a small amount of power from the charger so can get by on a lower-wattage charger . You can use a higher wattage charger on any MacBook—or even iPhone—as the device itself regulates the power input. 
 We recommend a 65W or faster charger for all but the MacBook Neo, which is fine with a 45W power adapter that will be faster than the supplied 20W Apple charger. That said, a tiny 45W charger is fine for a MacBook Air, too, if size is the most important factor for you. Go for 100W for the 14-inch MacBook Pro and 140W for the 16-inch Pro for the very fastest speeds.
 Fast Charging    
 Apple supports fast charging on all its latest MacBook models , except the Neo. When connected with the right charger and cable, you can charge a MacBook Air or Pro battery up to 50 per cent in 30 minutes. 
 While Apple doesn’t mention fast charging in relation to the MacBook Neo , we suspect that the 20W charger is a bare minimum and you should get faster charging using a 30W or faster charger. We will test this when we have a Neo in our hands. The Neo is the only modern MacBook that lacks a MagSafe 3 charging port.
 The MacBook Air models require a 70W charger, which effectively pushes you to 100W for a non-Apple charger.
 On the 14-inch MacBook Pro , you can fast-charge with a 96W or higher USB-C charger and USB-C to MagSafe 3 Cable or USB-C charge cable.
 On the 16-inch MacBook Pro , you can fast-charge only with an 140W USB-C Power Adapter (PD 3.1) paired with the USB-C to MagSafe 3 Cable (or a Thunderbolt 5 cable for the M4 and M5 models). Look for a power adapter that supports the latest PD 3.1 standard; other USB chargers have a practical maximum of 100W—fine for a 16-inch Pro but not as fast a charge.
 Power ports 
 More power ports on a charger make sense as we all have more than one device that needs charging. Look for the total power output if you want to charge more than one device at the same time. When you’re using your MacBook at full power, your charger might not have enough spare power for charging other devices unless you buy a charger with a higher wattage where the excess power can be channeled to your iPhone or AirPods at the same time as you power your laptop.

 Most multi-port chargers reserve specific maximum power output to each port, known as rules-based charging. The 10-port Plugable PS-10CC is the first USB-C charging station to use real-time intelligent software-based priority charging that distributes power across all connected devices—prioritized in the order you choose from left to right. As devices reach full charge, the now greater available power is reallocated down the line. As the first devices attain full battery status, the PS-10CC automatically shifts the excess power to the next set of connected devices, which should ensure that all receive the required power in the shortest possible time.
 While there’s a maximum of 100W of power available across the 10 charging ports at one time and some laptop might request that full 100W, commonly it will be far less—often ranging from 30-65W—so multiple laptops may charge at the same time in this scenario.

The top two USB-C are rated at 100W—with potential to fast-charge a 14-inch MacBook Pro or any size MacBook Air—with the third at 30W—enough to fast charge an iPhone or iPad. Below them are three 15W USB-A ports.
 Maximum power output from the USB ports is 100W, so that total needs to be spread around devices in using them at the same time. 100W is enough to charge a MacBook and an iPhone or iPad and maybe enough to power up your Apple Watch or AirPods case while you’re at it.

 There’s a lesser-powered 65W Charging Station ; also available in the U.K. and E.U., although those regions cap the number of AC sockets to two compared to three in the U.S. We’re less enamored of this 65W version not just because of the lower power but also the fact that there are more legacy USB-A ports than modern USB-C. You can’t fast-charge Apple devices from a USB-A port so we always prefer USB-C, with maybe one or two old-school USB-A ports there just in case.
 Choose the right USB-C cable 
 You need to connect the charger to your MacBook using a USB-C to USB-C charging cable or USB-C to MagSafe cable. (Note that the MacBook Neo doesn’t have a MagSafe port, so relies on USB-C cables for charging.)
 If your Mac has a MagSafe 3 port (14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro introduced in 2021; MacBook Air introduced in 2022), you can use Apple’s own USB-C to MagSafe 3 Cable (PD 3.1-supporting 240W maximum). As well as freeing up one of the MacBook’s Thunderbolt ports, this can protect from accidental cable pulls and is required for MacBook fast-charging on 16-inch MacBook Pro models that don’t boast Thunderbolt 5 ports. Apple’s MagSafe cable is expensive at $49 / £49 compared to a quality USB-C cable. Apple’s USB-C to USB-C charging cables (100W maximum) cost $19/£19 but you can find quality USB-C charging cables cheaper, for example from Ugreen ( Amazon.com / Amazon U.K. ).
 Few of the chargers reviewed here come with a USB-C cable. Of course, you can use the cable that shipped with your MacBook, but having a spare is always useful. We’ve rounded up the best USB-C and Thunderbolt cables .
 Best charger for MacBook Neo
 The MacBook Neo ships with a 20W Power Adapter . Apple doesn’t mention fast-charging as an opportunity for its new entry-level MacBook but we expect that it can accept more than a fairly puny 20W. There’s no need to go with a 65W or higher charger unless it has multiple ports, but a 45W charger such as the ultra-compact Anker Nano 45W Charger ( U.S. / U.K. ) is a great option, and over 50% smaller than Apple’s 30W charger. It’s more powerful than Apple’s 35W Power Adapter and less expensive. 
 Best charger for MacBook Air
 The MacBook Air ships with a choice of 40W Dynamic Power Adapter (with 60W Max boost), 35W Dual USB-C Port , or 70W USB-C . The 40/60W and dual 35W chargers are fine but you’ll need at least 70W for the fastest charging—which pushes you into 100W charger territory, although 65W/67W is surely close enough!
 For a 45W charger with just one port, the Anker Nano 45W Charger ( U.S. / U.K. ) is a decent choice. It has just the one port, but the amount of spare charge you’d get using a 35W charger with a MacBook Air isn’t likely to offer much if you are also trying to charge even your AirPods unless the laptop was sitting doing not much at all at the time. The Rolling Square 65W Supertiny charger ( U.S. / U.K. ) is just as small and offers more juice.
 Going for a 65W or even 100W multiport charger makes more sense. Anker’s three-port Anker Prime 67W GaN Wall Charger ( U.S. / U.K. ) can charge a laptop at 45W and an iPhone or iPad at 20W. It has two USB-C ports (both capable of PD charging at 65W, although not at the same time) and a 22.5W USB-A port. You could even charge a MacBook Air at 40W (still higher than Apple’s supplied charger), an iPhone at 12W and a set of AirPods at 5W. Or fast-charge an M2 MacBook Air.
 Ugreen’s 3-port Nexode Pro 65W USB-C Charger ( U.S. / U.K. ) is similar, although a smidge larger. Using all three ports, you could charge a laptop at 45W and two smaller devices at 15W shared.
 Best charger for 13-inch or 14-inch MacBook Pro
 The 13-inch MacBook Pro shipped with a 67W Power Adapter, so you can look to a 65W charger to save on money and size. You won’t notice the lost 2W.
 Your choice of charger for the 14-inch MacBook Pro depends on the model. The latest M5, M5 Pro and M5 Max 14-inch MacBook Pro models ship with a choice of 70W USB-C or 96W USB-C charger.
 Note that the M5 MacBook Pro models now ship without a charger in the U.K. and E.U.
 To make things simpler, just plan on matching any MacBook Pro with a 100W charger. A 65W charger will suffice, but you won’t get fast-charging like you will with a 100W model. Anker has the most affordable single-port charger, the 715 Nano II 65W ( U.S. / U.K. ). For a multiport 100W charger we rate Ugreen’s 4-port Nexode 100W USB-C Wall Charger ( U.S. / U.K. ) or the Anker 737 GaNPrime 120W Charger ( U.S. / U.K. ), which is smaller and has a higher total power output but features one less port. Very similar to the Ugreen 100W Charger is the Anker Prime 100W GaN Wall Charger ( U.S. / U.K. ), which both U.S. and U.K. users will appreciate for its foldable plug prongs.
 As well as fast-charging a 14in Pro using the 100W port, you can charge at full 65W power and have spare to charge another device at up to 30W, or charge the laptop a little slower and charge three other devices, say your iPhone, iPad and AirPods.
 Owners of the newer MacBook Pro with Thunderbolt 5 ports can use either Apple’s MagSafe 3 cable or any certified 240W USB-C cable to fast-charge their laptop. Older 16-inch models with Thunderbolt 4 ports must use the MagSafe 3 cable for fast charging but can still receive 100W of power from 100W USB-C cables. Simon Jary
 Best charger for 16-inch MacBook Pro
 Anker, Ugreen and Plugable have their own PD 3.1 fast-charging USB-C 140W chargers that are cheaper and smaller than Apple’s super-tall 140W Power Adapter ( U.S. / U.K. ). The best value is the $49.95 Plugable 140W USB-C Power Adapter .
 A 140W power adapter will fast-charge the 16-inch MacBook Pro (2021 and later models) from 0-50 percent charge in 30 minutes as it supports the most up-to-date PD 3.1 charing. The newer 16-inch MacBook Pro models (2024 and later) boast Thunderbolt 5 ports that support PD 3.1 so you can use 240W-certified USB-C cables as well as Apple’s expensive $49 USB-C to MagSafe 3 cable .
 For older 16‑inch MacBook Pro (2021 & 2023) the Thunderbolt 4 ports are PD 3.0 rated rather than 3.1, so you’ll need the Apple MagSafe 3 cable for 140W fast charging. 
 The Ugreen Nexode Pro 160W Charger ( U.S. / U.K. ) is much smaller than the Apple 140W charger and boasts four charging ports. Fast-charge the 16-inch MacBook using the top USB-C port, and luxuriate with 100W and 30W ports below, and a 22.5W USB-A port at the top—although remember that the maximum total output is 160W. As the most able PD 3.1 charger, we recommend this as a portable second charger for 16in MacBook Pro owners if they travel with their laptop a lot. The cheaper Anker 140W 4-Port PD 3.1 Charger ( U.S. / U.K. ) is interesting with its four downward-hanging ports but maxes at 140W compared to Ugreen’s 160W. The Anker Prime Charger ( U.S. / U.K. ) has just three downward ports but a 140W max.
 If you can live without the fast charging, a 100W charger should be ample for most situations, and here there are more options with multi-charging opportunities.
 Ugreen’s Nexode 100W USB-C Wall Charger ( U.S. / U.K. ) has four charging ports, but for a budget one-port 100W wall charger it’s hard to beat the Nekteck 100W USB-C Charger ( U.S ), which comes with its own 2m (6.5ft) USB-C cable.
 And, again, Ugreen’s powerful Nexode 200W USB-C Desktop Charger ( U.S. / U.K. ) is a great, if less portable, option.
 Which charger does each MacBook need?
 Here are the power specs of the batteries and power adapters that Apple ships with each of its MacBooks:
 MacBook Neo : 20W Power Adapter
 M1 MacBook Air : 30W Power Adapter
 M2 MacBook Air : 30W or 35W Power Adapter depending on 8-or-10-core GPU (Graphics Processing Unit); fast-charge capable with 70W charger or higher
 13-inch M3 MacBook Air : 30W or 35W Power Adapter depending on 8-or-10-core GPU (Graphics Processing Unit); fast-charge capable with 70W charger or higher
 13-inch M4 MacBook Air : 30W or 35W Power Adapter depending on 8-or-10-core GPU (Graphics Processing Unit); fast-charge capable with 70W charger or higher
 13-inch M5 MacBook Air : 40W Power Adapter; fast-charge capable with 70W charger or higher
 15-inch M3 MacBook Air : 35W Power Adapter; fast-charge capable with 70W charger or higher
 15-inch M4 MacBook Air : 35W Power Adapter; fast-charge capable with 70W charger or higher
 15-inch M5 MacBook Air : 40W Power Adapter; fast-charge capable with 70W charger or higher
 13-inch M1 MacBook Pro : 61W Power Adapter
 13-inch M2 MacBook Pro : 67W Power Adapter
 14-inch M2 Pro/Max MacBook Pro : 67W or 96W Power Adapter depending on 10-or-12-core GPU; fast-charge capable with 96W charger or higher
 14-inch M3 Pro/Max MacBook Pro : 70W or 96W Power Adapter depending on 14-or-16-core GPU; fast-charge capable with 96W charger or higher
 14-inch M4 Pro/Max MacBook Pro : 70W or 96W Power Adapter depending on 14-or-16-core GPU; fast-charge capable with 96W charger or higher
 14-inch M5, M5 Pro/Max MacBook Pro : 70W or 96W Power Adapter; fast-charge capable with 96W charger or higher
 15-inch MacBook Pro : 87W Power Adapter
 16-inch MacBook Pro : 140W Power Adapter fast-charger
 FAQ 
 1. 
 Can you use a charger with a higher wattage than your laptop?
 Yes, you can safely use a laptop charger with a higher wattage as the laptop will only ever draw the amount of power required at the time. If your laptop was supplied with a 35W charger it will never draw more than 35W unless being fast-charged, so you can use a 65W, 90W or higher charger. To reassure you even further, you can safely charge your 5W AirPods with a 240W charger if you wish.
 If the charger has multiple ports that extra juice will mean you can charge other devices at the same time.
 2. 
 Can you use a charger with a lower wattage than your laptop?
 You can but you should try to avoid using a lower wattage charger than what your laptop requires. A 30W charger can’t supply sufficient power for a 90W laptop’s needs. At the least, your laptop is likely to run out of power while you are using it. At the worst, you could damage the laptop or create dangerous problems for the charger.
 The under-powered charger won’t have enough power to give to your laptop and it therefore has to work harder to try to match the needs of your laptop. The danger is that this can cause overheating and potentially fire.
 For more details read our explainer What wattage USB-C charger can you use to charge a MacBook? 
 3. 
 Must I use Apple’s MagSafe 3 charging cable with a MacBook?
 Most modern MacBooks except the MacBook Neo feature a MagSafe 3 charging port, and ship with a 2m USB-C to MagSafe 3 cable, which otherwise cost a hefty $49 / £49 to buy separately. However, you can use a USB-C charging cable instead if you don’t have a MagSafe 3 cable to hand.
 Check the wattage rating of the USB-C charging cable, which are often rated at only up to 60W. If you need faster, look for at least a 100W USB-C charging cable, which is optimum for fast-charging all MacBook models except for the 16-inch MacBook Pro. That model requires 140W of power to fast-charge. Older (2021 -2023) 16-inch models have 100W Thunderbolt 4 ports so require the MagSafe 3 cable to fast-charge, but newer (2024) 16-inch Pros boast 240W Thunderbolt 5 ports so you can use any of the ports with a 240W-certified USB-C cable as an alternative.

MacBook Pro USB-C chargers: 96W for the 14-inch, 140W for the 16-inch | GearExplained Skip to content Image created with AI. The short version
 Apple lists a 96W or higher USB Power Delivery source for fast charging a 14-inch MacBook Pro, and 140W for a 16-inch. Fast charging means up to 50% in around 30 minutes.
 Some 14-inch M5 and M5 Pro models ship with a 70W adapter, which charges them but is below Apple's fast-charge figure.
 A 16-inch MacBook Pro needs a 140W USB PD 3.1 charger with a 28V step, plus Apple's MagSafe 3 cable or, on November 2023 and later models, a 240W USB-C cable. Chargers without the 28V step stop at about 100W.
 A MacBook Pro charges from one port at a time. Plugging a second charger into another port does not make it faster.
 Any USB-C charger that supports USB Power Delivery will charge a MacBook Pro. Apple says so on its power adapter page . The wattage decides how fast. Apple's MacBook Pro specifications call the 14-inch model fast-charge capable with a 96W or higher USB PD source, and the 16-inch with 140W or higher. Fast charging, in Apple's terms, is up to 50% in around 30 minutes.
 That is the number to shop for, and the charger in the box does not always meet it. Here are four chargers matched to it:
 Apple 140W USB-C Power Adapter for a 16-inch MacBook Pro.
 Apple 96W USB-C Power Adapter for a 14-inch MacBook Pro.
 Anker Prime Charger (100W, 3 Ports) for a smaller 14-inch charger that also has ports for a phone.
 UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W 5-Port for a desk charger that can fast charge a 16-inch model and charge other devices too.
 This guide is AI-generated from Apple, Anker and UGREEN documentation, measurements published by ChargerLAB, and the Wirecutter, Macworld and Tom's Hardware guides. GearExplained did not test these chargers. The product cards at the end link to Amazon, and GearExplained may earn a commission. That does not decide which chargers appear here.
 What each MacBook Pro asks for
 Find your model under Apple menu, About This Mac, or use Apple's identification page . Then match it here.
 MacBook Pro Adapter in the box Fast charging, per Apple Cable for fast charging 
 16-inch, 2021 or later 140W 140W adapter or USB PD source USB-C to MagSafe 3, or the 240W USB-C Charge Cable on November 2023 and later models 
 14-inch, M5 Pro 18-core or M5 Max 96W 96W or higher USB PD source USB-C to MagSafe 3 or a USB-C charge cable 
 14-inch, M5 or M5 Pro 15-core 70W 96W or higher USB PD source USB-C to MagSafe 3 or a USB-C charge cable 
 14-inch, 2021 to 2024 67W, 70W or 96W, depending on configuration Apple 96W or 140W adapter USB-C to MagSafe 3 or a USB-C charge cable 
 16-inch, 2019 Apple recommends 96W Not on Apple's fast-charge list USB-C charge cable 
 15-inch, 2016 or later Apple recommends 87W Not on Apple's fast-charge list USB-C charge cable 
 13-inch, 2016 or later Apple recommends 61W Not on Apple's fast-charge list USB-C charge cable 
 Source: Apple, MacBook Pro tech specs , Fast charge your MacBook Air or MacBook Pro and Use a power adapter with your Mac , checked October 21, 2026. For models before the M5 generation, the second column gives the adapters Apple's power adapter page recommends; check your own box or receipt for the one you got.
 The 70W adapter charges a 14-inch M5 but does not fast charge it. Apple ships the base M5 and the 15-core M5 Pro 14-inch models with the 70W adapter , and lists 96W or more for fast charging. ChargerLAB's M5 MacBook Pro test makes the same point: the laptop supports up to 96W, but the box holds a 70W adapter. In macOS Tahoe 26.4 or later, a Mac that is charging below its recommended wattage shows "Slow Charger" in the battery menu, according to Apple's charging page .
 The 16-inch needs more than a big number on the label. Charging above 100W uses USB Power Delivery 3.1 and a 28V step. ChargerLAB tested a 16-inch MacBook Pro with M4 Pro on Apple and third-party chargers . Apple's 140W adapter delivered about 139W at 27.88V. Most third-party chargers ran at 20V. Several that support PD 3.1 reached 28V and more than 126W, the highest at 134.8W. Macworld notes that chargers without PD 3.1 have a practical maximum of 100W. That still charges the 16-inch, just not at Apple's fast-charge rate.
 The cable matters on the 16-inch. Apple lists two adapter and cable pairings for fast charging it: the 140W adapter with the USB-C to MagSafe 3 Cable, or the 140W adapter with the 240W USB-C Charge Cable on the 16-inch MacBook Pro from November 2023 or later. For 2021 and early 2023 16-inch models, Apple lists only the MagSafe 3 cable. Macworld's MacBook charger guide puts the USB-C cutoff later, at the 2024 Thunderbolt 5 models. Apple's own list is the safer guide, and the MagSafe 3 cable works on every 16-inch from 2021 on.
 Two chargers do not add up. Apple says a Mac charges over only one port at a time and uses whichever source gives the most power. Plugging a second adapter into another port does not make it faster.

 1. Apple 140W USB-C Power Adapter: for the 16-inch MacBook Pro
 Apple 140W USB-C Power Adapter. Image: Apple 
 If you have a 16-inch MacBook Pro, this is the adapter Apple tests it with and the one it ships with. Apple's store page pairs it with the 16-inch model and a MagSafe 3 or 240W USB-C cable for up to 50% in around 30 minutes.
 ChargerLAB's charging review of a 16-inch MacBook Pro with M4 Pro measured it at about 139W. The laptop held about 139W for the first 22 minutes, reached 50% in 26 minutes and 80% in 51 minutes, and was full after 1 hour 41 minutes.
 It also covers a 14-inch MacBook Pro, which Apple fast charges from either its 96W or 140W adapter. It has one port, and Apple sells the cable separately.
 ChargerLAB's teardown of a newer version, Model A3607 with a 2026 production date, found the same exterior and dimensions as the 2021 Model A2452, about 95.7 by 74.4 by 28.5 mm, with prongs on a removable module and a 28V 5A step. Apple's store page lists the part number, MW2M3AM/A, but not which model a new unit carries.
 2. Apple 96W USB-C Power Adapter: for the 14-inch MacBook Pro
 Apple 96W USB-C Power Adapter. Image: Apple 
 Every 14-inch test note on Apple's fast-charge page , from the 2021 M1 Pro models to the 2026 M5 Pro and M5 Max, names this adapter, Model A2166. Apple's store page pairs it with the 14-inch MacBook Pro and either a MagSafe 3 cable or a USB-C charge cable.
 It is the straightforward upgrade if your 14-inch came with the 70W adapter. It is the wrong buy for a 16-inch. It will charge one, but Apple lists 140W for that model's fast charging, and ChargerLAB's 16-inch test shows chargers delivering about their rated power, like Apple's 87W adapter at 84.9W.
 Wirecutter's laptop charger guide describes it as 3.2 inches square and just over an inch thick, with fold-out prongs you can swap for a longer cord. Apple does not list its voltage steps, and it has one port. The cable is sold separately.
 3. Anker Prime Charger (100W, 3 Ports): a smaller charger for the 14-inch
 Anker Prime Charger (100W, 3 Ports, GaN). Image: Anker 
 Macworld recommends this charger for the 14-inch MacBook Pro. It is the charger to get if you want something smaller than Apple's 96W that can also charge a phone. Anker's product page lists 100W from either USB-C port on its own, at 20V 5A, which clears Apple's 96W fast-charge line. Anker gives 1.7 by 1.1 by 2.7 inches without the prongs and 6 ounces, and Macworld lists a foldable US plug.
 The catch is sharing. Anker lists 100W in total with two ports in use and 89W with all three, and says to put the laptop on the upper USB-C port. Once a phone is plugged in too, the MacBook gets less than 100W and can drop below Apple's fast-charge figure. Anker also recommends an e-marked cable for 100W, and no cable comes in the box.
 Make sure you get Model A2688. Anker's earlier Prime 100W charger, Model A2343, is a different design; Anker's support page for it puts the main USB-C port in the middle rather than at the top. Macworld points out that both USB-C ports on the A2688 top out at 100W, so it cannot fast charge a 16-inch model.
 4. UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W 5-Port: a desk charger that reaches 140W
 UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W 5-Port USB-C Charger. Image: UGREEN 
 For a 16-inch MacBook Pro on a desk with a phone and tablet beside it, UGREEN says this charger matches Apple's 140W adapter from a single port and adds four more ports. UGREEN's US product page says either C1 or C2 can supply up to 140W on its own, with 160W across all five ports. UGREEN claims it takes a 16-inch MacBook Pro with M4 Max to 56% in 30 minutes. That figure is UGREEN's own, and we found no independent MacBook Pro test of this exact model. ChargerLAB has tested it with an iPhone 18 Pro Max, covered in our iPhone charger guide .
 A rotating touch display shows total output, per-port power, the active charging protocol and temperature. UGREEN lists a two-year warranty and a foldable US plug, but no dimensions on its US page.
 Check the model. Macworld's pick for the 16-inch is the 4-port Nexode Pro 160W, which has one 140W port. This 5-port version, SKU 65636, lists two. As with any multiport charger, the 140W is available only while the other ports leave room for it. Tom's Hardware, which tested 20 chargers for its charger guide , found that every 100W-plus charger it tested throttled under sustained load.
 Which charger to buy for a MacBook Pro
 If you have a 16-inch MacBook Pro, buy Apple's 140W adapter, or the UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W 5-Port if you also want ports for other devices. Use Apple's MagSafe 3 cable. On a November 2023 or later 16-inch, a 240W USB-C cable also works.
 If you have a 14-inch MacBook Pro and the 70W adapter it came with feels slow, a 96W or 100W charger gives you Apple's fast-charge rate. Choose Apple's 96W adapter for the one Apple tested, or the Anker Prime 100W, Model A2688, for a smaller charger with spare ports.
 If you have a 13-inch or 15-inch MacBook Pro from 2016 on, or a 2019 16-inch, Apple lists no fast-charge mode. Match or beat the 61W, 87W or 96W Apple recommends for your model, and any of these chargers will do.
